title: Biome Identity and Edaphic Thresholds Shape Global Root‐Colonising Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungal Diversity
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

Arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi underpin diverse functions in terrestrial ecosystems. Root-colonising AM fungi constitute the symbiotically active fraction directly engaged in plant–fungal exchange. Yet global surveys remain predominantly soil-based, leaving the diversity patterns and drivers of these communities poorly resolved. We aimed to quantify global patterns in root-colonising AM fungal alpha diversity and to evaluate how environmental and host-related factors structure these patterns.

Location

Global.

Time Period

Published studies included in the GlobalAMFungi database up to 2021.

Major Taxa Studied

Root-colonising arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.

Methods

We analysed 3235 root samples from the GlobalAMFungi database, representing 394 host plant species worldwide. Alpha diversity was quantified using three Hill diversity metrics to capture richness and abundance-weighted diversity. We combined random forest modelling, SHAP-based variable interpretation and generalised additive mixed models to assess the relative contributions of biome context, edaphic conditions, climatic conditions and host attributes to variation in root-colonising AM fungal diversity.

Results

Root-colonising AM fungal diversity was structured by a clear hierarchy of ecological filters. Biome context framed broad-scale diversity patterns, while edaphic conditions outweighed climatic conditions. Among climatic predictors, moisture-related variables had stronger effects than temperature-related variables. Host attributes contributed less overall, although host phylogeny shaped abundance-weighted diversity. Key edaphic predictors showed pronounced non-linear relationships across Hill diversity metrics, with negative-to-positive transitions near 20–26 mg kg−1 for Olsen phosphorus, 10–11 for soil C:N ratio and pH 6.2–6.4.

Main Conclusions

Our study presents a global synthesis of the diversity and drivers of root-colonising AM fungal communities and highlights the primary roles of biome context and edaphic constraints in structuring their alpha diversity. These results establish empirical benchmarks for predicting their responses to environmental change and offer a root-centred complement to soil-based perspectives on AM fungal biogeography.
